title: William R. Berkley, Founder of W.R. Berkley Corporation, Dies at 80; His Son Becomes Chairman
summary: W.R. Berkley Corp. said its founder and executive chairman William R. Berkley died on June 9, 2026 at age 80, and that his son W. Robert Berkley Jr. was named chairman effective immediately, after a year of record earnings.
description:
William R. Berkley, the founder of the insurance group that bears his name, has died. W.R. Berkley Corporation said that its founder and executive chairman died on June 9, 2026 at the age of 80. Insurance Journal reported the news on June 10, together with the company's statement that his son, W. Robert Berkley Jr., has been named chairman, effective immediately. This article summarises that report and describes the company's background using the facts in it. An earlier version of this article stated that the company had a market value of about $25 billion, 8,804 employees and revenues of $14.7 billion, and that Berkley had started the business with $2,500 as a student. None of these figures appears in the Insurance Journal report, so they have been removed.

The facts of the announcement are short. The company, based in Greenwich, Connecticut, said that Berkley died on June 9. He founded the commercial property and casualty insurer in 1967 and built it into a Fortune 500 and S&P 500 company. AM Best, the rating agency for the insurance industry, gives the company an A+ financial strength rating. Berkley was chief executive of the insurance, reinsurance and monoline excess company until October 2015, when he handed control of its 60 businesses to his son. He stayed on as executive chairman and continued to attend the company's quarterly earnings calls, drawing on more than 50 years in the industry.

What made the company distinctive? In a call in November 2015, which was his last as chief executive, Berkley described the insurer as a large group of small niches. That phrase captures the business model. Instead of one large, centralised insurer, W.R. Berkley operates dozens of specialised underwriting units, each focused on a specific class of business, such as particular professional liability lines, excess and surplus lines, or specialty reinsurance. The idea is that experts in narrow areas can price risks better than generalists. He also said then, on pricing discipline, that the company does not look like the people it competes with, even though the numbers claim to be the same. In other words, the company tries to avoid chasing market prices when they are too low.

The business has performed strongly in recent years. According to the report, at the end of 2025 the company reported record fourth-quarter operating income of $450 million, record full-year net income of $1.8 billion and record full-year operating income of $1.7 billion. Operating income excludes certain items such as investment gains and losses, so it is a measure of the underlying insurance business. These results came in a period when specialty insurance rates rose for several years, though prices have recently softened in many lines, as the WTW survey of specialty rates shows. W.R. Berkley's focus on underwriting discipline will be tested in a softer market.

Succession has been planned for a decade. W. Robert Berkley Jr. has led the company as chief executive since 2015, and his appointment as chairman means he now holds both roles. In the company's statement he said he was deeply saddened by the passing of his father, who he described as a father, best friend and mentor to him and to numerous colleagues. The change in chairmanship is effective immediately, which means the board continues without a vacancy. The report does not say that any other leadership changes are planned.

For readers unfamiliar with the terms, a monoline excess insurer covers only one type of risk above the limits of other insurers' policies, while reinsurance is insurance bought by insurers to spread their own risks. W.R. Berkley operates in these specialised corners of the market, where policies are often complex and where underwriting judgement matters more than volume. That is one reason the founder's emphasis on niches and discipline has been so closely associated with the company's reputation among investors and competitors.

Berkley was also known for philanthropy. The report says he supported educational institutions and healthcare, including hospitals, research and communities. The report does not give amounts or names of the institutions.

How might this affect the company and the industry? The immediate effect on operations is likely to be limited, because the founder had handed day-to-day control to his son in 2015 and the business is run through many separate units with their own management. For investors, one question is whether the founder's influence on culture and strategy continues, which will become visible in how the company handles the softening market. For the specialty insurance market, the company is a significant underwriter and reinsurer, and its behaviour on pricing is closely watched.

The loss of a founder who built a company over nearly six decades is notable for the whole industry. His career spanned the growth of the excess and surplus market, several insurance cycles and the development of specialty underwriting as a discipline. Readers who want to follow the company can consult its regulatory filings and earnings releases.

key_points: William R. Berkley, founder and executive chairman of W.R. Berkley Corp., died on June 9, 2026 at age 80, the company said.
He founded the Greenwich, Connecticut-based commercial property and casualty insurer in 1967 and built it into a Fortune 500 and S&P 500 company rated A+ by AM Best.
He was chief executive until October 2015, when he handed control of its 60 businesses to his son, W. Robert Berkley Jr., who was named chairman effective immediately.
At the end of 2025 the company reported record fourth-quarter operating income of $450 million and record full-year net income of $1.8 billion and operating income of $1.7 billion.
Berkley described the company as 'a large group of small niches' and supported education and healthcare institutions.
why_it_matters: W.R. Berkley is one of the largest US specialty insurers, built on small, specialised businesses and tight underwriting. The orderly succession matters to employees, investors and the specialty insurance market it serves.

title: AM Best Warns of 'Warning Signs' in the D&O Market: Loss Ratio Up Five Points to 54.5 and Reserves for 2023 and 2024 Look Short
summary: AM Best says the US directors and officers liability line posted a fourth year of premium decline in 2025 while its direct loss ratio rose five points to 54.5 and reserves for accident years 2023 and 2024 proved inadequate.
description:
Directors and officers (D&O) liability insurance, which protects company leaders against claims that they mismanaged a business, has been a comfortable market for buyers. Premiums have fallen for years, capacity has been abundant and insurers have generally been profitable. A new analysis from the rating agency AM Best, reported by Insurance Journal on June 8, 2026, suggests that the good times may be fading. This article summarises that report. An earlier version of this article quoted several figures, including a 2021 premium peak, a 33% decline and a 49.0 prior-year loss ratio, that do not appear in the Insurance Journal article, so they have been removed. The article also contains no figures on expenses, competition or securities class action filings, and none are given here.

The first point is premiums. According to the report, 2025 was the fourth straight year of premium decline in the D&O line. Insurers had favourable direct underwriting results over the last few years, and buyers got competitive renewal terms and new product offerings in a market with abundant capacity. In 2025, premium decreases at renewal were smaller on average, and some accounts saw flat or slightly higher rates. AM Best says the decline in premiums may reflect lower demand, particularly for coverage tied to transactions, because fewer companies went public. The market for initial public offerings rebounded in 2025 but has since levelled off somewhat, which AM Best attributes to economic uncertainty linked to the conflict involving Iran.

The second point is claims. The direct loss ratio, which measures claims as a share of premiums, was 54.5 in 2025, five percentage points higher than in 2024. That is still a profitable number on its own, but the direction matters. More concerning, according to AM Best, is that reserves for accident years 2023 and 2024 turned out to be inadequate in 2025. An accident year groups claims by the year in which the event occurred, and reserves are the funds the insurer sets aside to pay them. If reserves have to be increased later, it means earlier results were better than they should have appeared, a pattern known as adverse development.

The report also notes that claims for accident years 2023 and 2024 are closing more slowly than for 2018 and 2019. Those two earlier years, AM Best says, caused adverse development in the last decade. Slower closure means claims stay open longer, and AM Best warns that it could erode profit margins as the eventual cost becomes clearer. D&O is a long-tail line: lawsuits can take years to resolve, so the full cost of a year's business is not known for a long time. That is why an insurer can report strong results for years and then face a reversal.

David Blades, an associate director at AM Best, described these as warning signs that might indicate an underlying deficiency that could lead to a downturn in D&O liability underwriting results in the near term. AM Best expects shrinking underwriting margins and a tighter environment for buyers in 2026. It also notes insurers' discipline on policy terms and conditions, and says insurers will need to conduct expert due diligence in choosing which industries and segments to write.

What are the headwinds? AM Best lists geopolitical and economic uncertainty, technology, and regulatory scrutiny. It says corporate leaders face criticism over how they handled trade policy, supply chains, overseas conflicts, changes to financial reporting, cyber risk and regulatory shifts such as those on environmental, social and diversity policies. Artificial intelligence adds disclosure and oversight risks. Some companies may struggle to link their AI investments to returns, which can lead to shareholder claims that statements about AI were misleading. AM Best says disclosure management will be vital to successful AI use in any industry.

What does it mean for buyers? A firmer market means that companies renewing D&O cover could see smaller premium reductions, flat renewals or increases, and tighter terms, depending on their industry, financial health and claims history. Companies should start renewal discussions early, prepare clear information about governance and AI-related disclosures, and compare options across markets. Boards should also review the limits they hold, and whether separate Side A cover for personal protection when the company cannot indemnify them is adequate.

What does it mean for insurers? The report is a reminder that profitable years may be overstated if reserves are not strong enough. Insurers that cut prices to win business in a competitive market could find that the cost of past years emerges later. The reaction of the market will depend on how reserves develop and on whether new entrants hold to underwriting discipline.

This summary reflects a rating agency's view of a segment, not a forecast for any specific company. Readers should consult AM Best's own report for the full analysis, and brokers for advice on their coverage.
image_alt: Directors and officers liability insurance and corporate governance (illustrative)
key_points: AM Best's analysis, reported by Insurance Journal on June 8, 2026, says 2025 was the fourth straight year of premium decline in the D&O line.
The direct loss ratio was 54.5 in 2025, five percentage points higher than in 2024.
Reserves for accident years 2023 and 2024 were inadequate in 2025, and claims for those years are closing more slowly than for 2018 and 2019.
David Blades of AM Best said the trends 'might indicate an underlying deficiency' that could lead to a downturn in D&O underwriting results in the near term.
Headwinds include geopolitical and economic uncertainty, technology, regulatory scrutiny and AI disclosure risk; AM Best expects shrinking margins and a tighter environment for buyers in 2026.
why_it_matters: D&O insurance protects company leaders and boards against lawsuits. After years of cheap, abundant cover, AM Best's warning suggests buyers should expect firmer terms, and it shows how slow-developing claims can undermine apparently profitable years.

title: Howard Hughes Holdings Completes Its $2.1 Billion Purchase of Vantage Group, Bringing Bill Ackman's Insurance Strategy to Life
summary: Howard Hughes Holdings closed its roughly $2.1 billion all-cash acquisition of Bermuda-based specialty insurer Vantage on June 4, 2026, funded by cash and $1 billion of preferred stock issued to Pershing Square Holdings, with Pershing Square managing the investments fee-free.
description:
A real estate developer has become an insurance group. On June 4, 2026, Howard Hughes Holdings completed its acquisition of Vantage Group Holdings, a Bermuda-based specialty insurer and reinsurer, in an all-cash transaction valued at about $2.1 billion. The closing, reported by Insurance Journal on June 5, is the most concrete step so far in an effort by the company's executive chairman, the investor Bill Ackman, to turn Howard Hughes into a diversified holding company. This article summarises that report. An earlier version of this article stated price-to-book multiples and mentioned insurance ratings that the report does not include, so they have been removed, and it described the investment arrangement as copying Berkshire Hathaway's approach in a way the companies describe differently, so the wording has been revised.

The deal facts are as follows. The buyer is Howard Hughes Holdings Inc., acting through a wholly owned subsidiary called Howard Hughes Insurance Holdings. The target is Vantage Group Holdings Ltd., which was founded in 2020 and was backed by the private equity firms Carlyle Group and Hellman & Friedman, who were the sellers. The acquisition was announced in December 2025 and closed on June 4, 2026, after all required regulatory approvals were received. The price is about $2.1 billion, all in cash. The companies say Vantage's existing leadership, go-to-market strategy, distribution model and service standards will continue, and Greg Hendrick remains its chief executive.

Funding came from two sources. Howard Hughes used its cash on hand and issued $1 billion of non-voting exchangeable perpetual preferred stock to Pershing Square Holdings, the listed investment vehicle associated with Ackman's firm. Preferred stock is a form of capital that ranks ahead of common shares for payments but does not carry votes, and 'perpetual' means it has no fixed maturity. The report also says that Howard Hughes will make a $200 million capital infusion in connection with the closing, which strengthens the insurer's balance sheet.

The investment arrangement is the unusual feature. Pershing Square Capital Management will manage Vantage's investment portfolio on a fee-free basis, and no additional investment management or advisory fees will be paid. For an insurer, investment income on premiums held before claims are paid is a major source of earnings, and the quality of that investing matters. Ackman is the founder and chief executive of Pershing Square and the executive chairman of Howard Hughes, so the arrangement links the insurer's investments to a manager who also controls the buyer. Ryan Israel, Howard Hughes's chief investment officer, is quoted in the report. Investors may weigh the benefit of no fees against the concentration and the potential conflicts of interest, which would normally be addressed through governance rules, but the report does not describe them.

The strategy behind the deal is explained in the executives' own words. Ackman said Vantage will now become the cornerstone of Howard Hughes' transformation into a diversified holding company. Israel said the company believes Vantage will generate high returns on equity for Howard Hughes' shareholders for decades to come. Hendrick called the closing the beginning of an exciting next chapter, and said Howard Hughes brings the permanent capital and the long-term horizon this business deserves. The phrase 'permanent capital' refers to the fact that a holding company does not have to return money to fund investors on a fixed schedule, in contrast with private equity funds that sell businesses after several years. The companies also say holding-company ownership is expected to strengthen Vantage's credit profile and underwriting flexibility, and that the focus will be on underwriting profitability rather than growth.

The report does not give Vantage's premium volume, profit, ratings or valuation multiples, so readers cannot judge the price from it. Those figures would be in the company's investor materials and filings. The advisers named give a sense of the scale: Jefferies advised Howard Hughes, with Latham & Watkins as legal counsel and Oliver Wyman as actuarial adviser, while J.P. Morgan Securities advised Vantage and Debevoise & Plimpton advised the sellers.

What are the risks? Specialty insurance and reinsurance are cyclical, and prices have been softening in many lines, as seen in recent Florida reinsurance renewals and in falling commercial rates in several markets. Success will depend on discipline in underwriting and on the performance of the investment portfolio. A holding company that combines real estate with insurance also has to manage its capital across very different businesses, and rating agencies and regulators will look at the group structure.

For the wider market, the deal is an example of private equity owners selling insurers that were built in the last cycle, and of buyers looking for insurance earnings and float. It follows other cross-border and strategic deals this year, including DB Insurance's purchase of Fortegra and Berkshire Hathaway's stake in Tokio Marine. Whether the Howard Hughes model delivers the returns the executives describe will take years to show, and investors will follow Vantage's results and Howard Hughes' disclosures for evidence.
image_alt: Holding company insurance acquisition and reinsurance deal (illustrative)
key_points: Howard Hughes Holdings completed its roughly $2.1 billion all-cash acquisition of Vantage Group Holdings on June 4, 2026, after announcing it in December 2025 and receiving all regulatory approvals.

The purchase was funded with cash on hand and $1 billion of non-voting exchangeable perpetual preferred stock issued to Pershing Square Holdings; HHH will also make a $200 million capital infusion at closing.
Pershing Square Capital Management will manage Vantage's investment portfolio on a fee-free basis, with no additional management or advisory fees.
Vantage, a Bermuda-based specialty insurer and reinsurer founded in 2020 and sold by Carlyle and Hellman & Friedman, keeps its leadership team under CEO Greg Hendrick and its distribution model.

Bill Ackman, HHH's executive chairman, called Vantage the cornerstone of Howard Hughes' transformation into a diversified holding company; the companies emphasise underwriting profitability over growth.
why_it_matters: Insurance float, the money held between collecting premiums and paying claims, can be invested for the long term. The deal tests whether a real estate developer can become an insurance-led holding company in the style of Berkshire Hathaway, and shows how private-equity-backed insurers are being sold.

title: Acrisure to Cut About 2,250 Jobs, 11% of Its Workforce, Citing AI, as Broker Growth Slows
summary: Acrisure CEO Greg Williams told staff on May 20 that about 2,250 jobs, around 11% of the company's roughly 19,000 employees, would go by the end of 2027, citing AI and digital platforms, following 400 accounting job cuts announced in October 2025.
description:
Acrisure, one of the largest insurance brokers in the United States, is cutting about 2,250 jobs and attributing the change to artificial intelligence and digital platforms. The decision was set out in a memo from chief executive Greg Williams, reported by Insurance Journal on May 22, 2026. This article summarises that report. An earlier version of this article gave a workforce of 19,000 as a fact from the company, a valuation above $30 billion, a revenue figure near $5 billion and an organic growth rate of 5.9% for US retail brokers. Only the 19,000 figure, drawn from the company's website, and the $2.8 billion property and casualty revenue appear in the Insurance Journal article, so the other figures have been removed. Acrisure did not immediately respond to the publication's request for comment.

The numbers and timing are as follows. About 2,250 employees will leave the company by the end of 2027, which is roughly 11% of headcount, and the majority are in the United States. Acrisure has about 19,000 team members according to its website. Layoffs started on May 21 and will continue in phases into 2027. This is not the first round. In October 2025, Acrisure announced 400 layoffs in its accounting workforce and cited technology and AI advances at that time too. The two announcements show a pattern of using automation to reduce back-office roles.

Williams's memo explains the reasoning. He said Acrisure is entering what he called a new phase of execution. Technology, AI and digital platforms are changing how businesses operate and how clients expect to be served, he wrote, and the company made its first scaled AI investment in 2020. Going forward, Acrisure will combine human expertise with technology platforms, use AI and automation to reduce manual work, and build digital capacity for clients. He described the biggest risk as not acting decisively enough and seeking comfort in the way things used to be. He also said North American insurance operations would be organised more deliberately around lines of business.

The company is based in Grand Rapids, Michigan, and is backed by private equity. It ranked third in Insurance Journal's 2025 list of the Top 100 Independent Property/Casualty Agencies, with about $2.8 billion in property and casualty revenue. Insurance brokers sell policies on behalf of customers and earn commissions or fees. Over the last decade, private equity funds have bought many brokers and combined them, expecting steady growth in commissions as insurance prices rose.

An industry observer in the article, Kevin Stipe, chief executive of the consultancy Reagan, explained why this is happening now. Private equity models generally depend on high growth and acquisitions. Citing S&P Global, he said Acrisure's North American organic growth, which is growth from existing businesses without counting acquisitions, was only about 1% to 2% last year. Because Acrisure carries debt, he said, it is under more pressure to address profit margins than firms without debt, and it has to respond faster and more strongly. He saw the cuts as part of a broader trend of slowing growth for brokers.

That trend has a clear cause. Commission income is linked to premium levels. When insurance prices rise quickly, brokers grow even without winning new customers. In 2025 and 2026, prices in many commercial lines have been flat or falling, as other articles in this series show, for example the softening of specialty rates and falling property catastrophe reinsurance prices. With less help from price increases, brokers have to find growth elsewhere or lower costs.

What does the move say about AI and jobs in insurance? Brokerage and insurance operations include many tasks such as processing certificates, handling renewals and entering data, which technology can automate. Acrisure's memo is one of the clearest statements by a major insurance employer that AI is a reason for job cuts. Other industry leaders have been more cautious. For example, the head of the broker Marsh, discussing artificial intelligence on a recent call, focused on how AI risks should be insured and not on staffing. It is too early to know how far automation will reduce employment in the industry, and how many new roles will be created in data, risk analysis and client advisory work.

What should clients expect? In principle, automation can speed up service and lower costs, but clients may notice changes in who handles their accounts. Businesses that rely on a broker should ask how service levels will be maintained and who their contacts will be. For employees across the industry, the story signals the need for skills that are harder to automate, such as complex risk advice and relationship management.

The report does not say how the cuts will be spread across functions or locations, what severance will be provided, or what savings Acrisure expects. Those details, and any response from the company, will determine how the restructuring is judged.
image_alt: Insurance brokerage firm and AI workforce transformation (illustrative)
key_points: Acrisure will cut about 2,250 employees, roughly 11% of headcount and mostly in the US, by the end of 2027, according to a memo from CEO Greg Williams; layoffs began on May 21, 2026 and will continue in phases.

The company has about 19,000 team members, is based in Grand Rapids, Michigan, is private-equity backed and ranked third in Insurance Journal's 2025 Top 100 Independent P/C Agencies with about $2.8 billion of P/C revenue.
Williams said technology, AI and digital platforms are changing how businesses operate and clients are served, and that the biggest risk is not acting decisively enough.
In October 2025 Acrisure announced 400 layoffs in its accounting workforce, also citing technology and AI.

Kevin Stipe of Reagan, citing S&P Global, said Acrisure's North American organic growth was only about 1% to 2% last year and that debt puts pressure on margins; he sees slowing growth across brokers.
why_it_matters: Insurance brokers have grown through acquisitions and steady price increases. As organic growth slows, large brokers are turning to automation to protect margins, which is changing the jobs available in insurance distribution.

title: Florida's June 2026 Reinsurance Renewals: Catastrophe Rates Fall 15% to 20% as Insurers' Surplus Rises 45%
summary: Guy Carpenter says June 2026 Florida property-catastrophe reinsurance prices fell by roughly 15% to 20% risk-adjusted as demand rose 12%, helped by a 76.8% combined ratio in 2025, 45% higher policyholder surplus and tort reform.
description:
Florida's property insurance market, which was in crisis only a few years ago, has entered a calmer phase. According to Insurance Journal's May 29, 2026 report on Guy Carpenter's review of the June 1 renewals, prices for catastrophe reinsurance, the cover that insurers buy to protect themselves from large hurricane losses, fell again, capacity was plentiful and terms improved. This article summarises that report. An earlier version of this article also cited catastrophe bond issuance figures and comments by another broker, Howden Re, that do not appear in the Insurance Journal article, so those have been removed.

The headline is price. Guy Carpenter says property-catastrophe prices kept softening, with risk-adjusted decreases typically in the range of 15% to 20%. Risk-adjusted means that the change is measured after allowing for differences in the risk covered, so it compares like with like. Some individual layers saw deeper reductions, especially at remote attachment points, which are the higher layers that are only hit by the largest storms and had been among the most expensive in prior years. The loads for reinstatement premium protection, a feature that lets an insurer restore its cover after a loss, eased from what the report calls very elevated recent levels.

Demand rose too. Property-catastrophe demand increased by 12%, according to the report, driven by depopulation of Citizens Property Insurance Corporation, the state-backed insurer of last resort, along with population growth and higher average insured values. Reinsurers responded by broadening their risk appetite across attachment points and showing willingness to expand cover. Capacity for lower-attaching catastrophe layers and for reinstatement premium protection was abundant, after being constrained in recent years. The report says incumbent reinsurers showed such strong appetite that it was hard for new entrants to win shares on programmes. Interest in subsequent event cover grew, and collateralised reinsurers more often offered combined packages such as top-and-drop and top-and-aggregate structures.

Quota share arrangements, in which a reinsurer takes a fixed percentage of an insurer's business, moved in a different direction. Demand for quota share from Florida insurers fell as their balance sheets strengthened, because they no longer needed the capital relief, but reinsurers' appetite for Florida quota share rose. Terms improved for insurers, including more catastrophe occurrence limit, more catastrophe aggregate limit and higher ceding commission.

What explains the recovery? The report points to profitability and capital. Domestic Florida underwriters posted a 76.8% combined ratio in 2025. A combined ratio below 100 means an underwriting profit, so 76.8 is very strong. The 2025 hurricane season was the first in a decade without a landfalling tropical storm in Florida, which helped results. Policyholders' surplus, the capital insurers hold above their liabilities, rose 45%, allowing many insurers to retain more risk themselves and negotiate better reinsurance terms.

Legal reform is the second factor. The report says landmark tort reforms were enacted in December 2022, and that litigation has fallen about 66% from its peak. The reforms included changes to the rules on attorney fees, which had encouraged lawsuits over property claims. A separate recent report, cited in the article, estimates that Florida property and casualty insurance costs are about 14.5% lower than they would have been without the reforms. These statistics come from the industry and reflect the reforms' supporters' analysis; consumer advocates have raised concerns about reduced claimant rights, a debate that the report does not cover.

Citizens' role is changing. More than 1.4 million policies have left Citizens since 2022, according to the report, and depopulation has helped launch 14 new companies over the past three years. Guy Carpenter's Florida expert says the depopulation era has largely ended as of early 2026, and that growth will now rely on normal market competition. The firm also said reinsurers want to grow with their Florida clients and that policyholders are starting to see rate relief.

How much of this reaches homeowners? Reinsurance is one of insurers' biggest costs in Florida, so lower prices should in time help moderate premium increases, but the article does not quantify any effect on consumer prices, and rates depend on many factors including claims, building costs and regulatory approval. The signal is that the pressure that drove insurers out of the state and pushed Citizens to a huge size has eased.

The risks remain. A quiet hurricane season and low litigation have produced a strong run of results, but the market is still highly exposed to a major storm, and prices in a soft market can fall too far. A direct hit on a populated area would test reserves, reinsurance programmes and the new insurers that have entered the market. For that reason, observers will watch the hurricane season, claims frequency and whether insurers keep their underwriting discipline as competition returns.

For investors and policymakers, the renewal results show a market that has gone from stress to recovery within a few years, and the story is mostly about capital and law reform. For homeowners, the best advice is to compare quotes, review wind and flood coverage, and keep hurricane preparations in place regardless of how the market is performing.
image_alt: Florida coastal property insurance and reinsurance market recovery (illustrative)
key_points: Guy Carpenter's June 2026 review, reported by Insurance Journal on May 29, says property-catastrophe prices kept softening, with risk-adjusted decreases typically in the 15% to 20% range and deeper cuts on some remote layers.
Property-catastrophe demand rose 12%, driven by Citizens depopulation, population growth and higher insured values, and reinsurers broadened their appetite across attachment points.
Domestic Florida underwriters posted a 76.8% combined ratio in 2025, and policyholders' surplus rose 45%, letting many insurers retain more risk and negotiate better terms.
Litigation has fallen about 66% from its peak after the December 2022 tort reforms, and a separate report estimates Florida property and casualty costs are about 14.5% lower than without them.
More than 1.4 million policies have left Citizens since 2022 and 14 new companies launched in three years, but Guy Carpenter says the depopulation era has largely ended.
why_it_matters: Florida is the most exposed major hurricane market in the United States. Cheaper reinsurance lowers insurers' costs, which can eventually ease pressure on homeowners' premiums, but results still depend on whether the hurricane season stays quiet.

title: Merck Settles Gardasil Lawsuits for More Than $50 Million: What the Deal Covers and What It Does Not Admit
summary: Merck will pay more than $50 million, according to people familiar with the matter, to settle more than 200 dismissed North Carolina cases and a Los Angeles case set for trial, ending Gardasil litigation apart from one case without admitting liability.
description:
Merck has agreed to settle most of the lawsuits over its Gardasil human papillomavirus vaccine, ending a long-running piece of product liability litigation without admitting that the vaccine caused harm. The settlement, reported by Insurance Journal on June 8, 2026, is for more than $50 million according to people familiar with the matter. This article summarises that report. An earlier version of this article described the claims in a way that implied a federal summary judgment ruling in March 2025 and gave details of appeals that the report does not support. The report describes a ruling by a North Carolina judge, and those details have been corrected here. The report does not discuss insurance coverage, so this article does not attempt to say who is paying beyond the company's statements.

The numbers first. Merck will pay more than $50 million to settle more than 200 cases, according to people familiar with the matter. The company says the amount is considerably less than its anticipated costs of defending the cases, and it calls the payment not material to the company. Those statements are consistent with a business decision to end the litigation, not an admission that the claims had merit. Merck says it decided to end the litigation in its entirety by settling, and officials say the deal will only be finalised if enough people who received Gardasil sign on. In its February annual report, Merck said it had entered into a proposed agreement in October 2025 that still needed additional steps.

What cases does it cover? The settlement covers all Gardasil litigation except one case, according to the report. The more than 200 cases in North Carolina were dismissed last year by a judge who found them preempted by the Food and Drug Administration's approval of the vaccine's labelling, and who also found the plaintiffs' expert evidence insufficient. Preemption is a legal doctrine under which federal law overrides state-law claims; in drug cases, defendants argue that they could not have changed the label without FDA approval, so a claim that the label was inadequate cannot succeed under state law. Those dismissed cases are included in the deal. The other major piece is Robi v. Merck, case number BC628589, in the Superior Court of California for the County of Los Angeles. The plaintiff, Jennifer Robi, says Gardasil, which she received as a teenager, caused a heart ailment that left her in a wheelchair. The case was set for trial next month, and it could have produced the first jury decision against Merck over the vaccine. According to the report, the Los Angeles lawyer for the plaintiff declined to comment.

The report also mentions a connection that has drawn attention. Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the US Secretary of Health and Human Services, is a former plaintiffs' lawyer who helped prepare Robi's claims before becoming secretary in 2025. He was set to receive 10% referral fees on successful Gardasil suits but has waived them. The report notes that in March a judge temporarily blocked his effort to reduce the list of recommended childhood vaccines, including a proposal to cut the recommended HPV doses for young people from up to three to one, and that Kennedy and the group Children's Health Defense are appealing. We note these points as reported and do not draw conclusions about them.

Merck's position on safety is consistent. It has consistently denied that the vaccine causes dangerous side effects, and it says its research continues to support the safety and efficacy of its HPV vaccines. The settlement does not require a finding that the vaccine was harmful. Gardasil prevents HPV infection, which researchers have linked to cervical cancer. The vaccine has been approved in about 150 countries since its introduction 20 years ago, and Merck says more than 900 million doses of Gardasil and Gardasil 9 have been distributed worldwide.

On the business side, Gardasil sales reached $8.9 billion in 2023. They have declined over the last two years because of low-cost competitors in China, after strong growth in the early 2020s. For Merck, which is based in Rahway, New Jersey, the settlement removes a source of uncertainty and cost from a product whose revenue is under pressure.

Why does this matter to the insurance and risk community? Mass tort litigation, where many plaintiffs sue over the same product, is a significant driver of liability costs for manufacturers and their insurers, and it features in the discussion of social inflation, the rise in claim costs from legal and social factors. The settlement illustrates three features of such disputes. Defendants with strong legal defences, such as preemption, may still settle to avoid the unpredictability of a jury trial. Settlement amounts can be modest compared with the cost of defending cases over many years. And the outcome of a few bellwether cases can influence the value of hundreds of others. Our coverage this week of the Swiss Re Institute's report on UK liability claims shows similar themes in another jurisdiction.

For patients and parents, the settlement says nothing about whether to vaccinate; medical guidance on HPV vaccination comes from public health authorities and doctors. For investors, the key points are the size of the payment relative to Merck's earnings and the risk that remains from the one case not covered. Readers should consult Merck's regulatory filings for the company's own description of the matter.
key_points: Merck will pay more than $50 million to settle Gardasil product liability claims, according to people familiar with the matter, an amount it says is considerably less than its anticipated cost of defending the cases.

The deal covers more than 200 North Carolina cases that a judge dismissed last year as preempted by FDA approval of the vaccine's labelling, and Robi v. Merck in Los Angeles Superior Court, which was set for trial next month.
Merck does not admit liability and says its research continues to support the safety and efficacy of its HPV vaccines; the settlement does not require a finding that the vaccine was harmful.
Officials say the deal will only be finalised if enough people who received Gardasil sign on; Merck said in February it had a proposed agreement from October 2025 that needed more steps.

Gardasil sales reached $8.9 billion in 2023 and have declined over two years because of low-cost Chinese competitors; more than 900 million doses of Gardasil and Gardasil 9 have been distributed worldwide.
why_it_matters: Product liability litigation is a major cost for drugmakers and a large source of liability insurance exposure. The case also shows how federal preemption defences can shape outcomes and why companies sometimes settle ahead of a first jury trial.

title: UAE Health Insurance: A $10.1 Billion Segment in 2026, Falling Commercial Rates and the Worker Cover Scheme That Began on January 1, 2025
summary: Khaleej Times reports the UAE health and medical insurance segment is projected at about $10.11 billion in 2026 and $15.04 billion by 2031, while Gulf News details the Dh320 basic employer-funded cover for private-sector and domestic workers that began on January 1, 2025.
description:
Health insurance in the United Arab Emirates is expanding on two fronts: a growing market for medical cover, and a rule that requires employers to insure most workers. This article combines two reports. The first is a Khaleej Times article of February 17, 2026 on pricing and demand, and the second is a Gulf News explainer published on January 1, 2025 on the national scheme for workers. An earlier version of this article described a mandatory scheme with a specific cost trend of 11.3% for 2026, an assertion that the UAE has the highest insurance penetration in the Gulf region and a count of more than 60 licensed insurers. Those statements do not appear in the reports reviewed, so they have been removed.

Start with the size of the market. Khaleej Times says the health and medical insurance segment is projected to reach about $10.11 billion in 2026, and to grow at a compound annual rate of 8.26% to about $15.04 billion by 2031. The article says motor and property and casualty lines are expected to grow too but gives no figures for them. It also says the sector is set for sustained double-digit expansion in 2026, but does not attribute that claim to a source, so it should be treated as a general statement rather than a forecast. The International Monetary Fund expects UAE economic growth of about 5% in 2026, which supports demand. Swiss Re is quoted as saying the Middle East, including the UAE, is among the fastest-growing insurance markets in the world, and S&P Global Ratings expects continued growth with consolidation among smaller players and disciplined underwriting.

Prices for commercial insurance are moving the other way. The article cites Marsh's Global Insurance Market Index, under which global commercial insurance rates fell an average of 4% in the fourth quarter of 2025. In India, the Middle East and Africa, the fall was sharper, at 10%. Middle East property rates fell about 11% on average, the largest decline in the region, global casualty rates fell about 5%, and UAE casualty pricing stayed largely stable. Directors and officers liability rates in the UAE and Saudi Arabia fell 15% to 20%, and cyber premiums in the Middle East fell 5% to 10%. Omar Gemei of Marsh, who leads global placement for India, the Middle East and Africa, is named in the article as a source. These figures concern commercial lines such as property and liability, not individual health policies, but they show a competitive market in which buyers benefit.

Regulation is changing too. The Central Bank of the UAE is implementing reforms under Federal Decree-Law No. 48 of 2023, which cover solvency, governance and consumer protection. The article says the reforms are expected to encourage consolidation and improve transparency. Sukoon Insurance is named among the insurers in the article. Those points matter for health insurance because smaller insurers that cannot meet higher standards may merge or exit, and customers may see fewer but stronger providers.

Now to the workers' scheme, as described by Gulf News on January 1, 2025. The newspaper says the nationwide requirement took effect that day. It was introduced by the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation in December 2024 and approved by the UAE Cabinet. It requires employers to provide health insurance for all private-sector employees in every emirate and for all domestic workers. Abu Dhabi and Dubai already had mandatory insurance, and the policy extends the requirement to Sharjah, Ajman, Umm Al Quwain, Ras Al Khaimah and Fujairah. Workers with valid permits issued before January 1, 2025 are exempt until their permits come up for renewal, when insurance becomes mandatory. The Federal Authority for Identity, Citizenship, Customs and Port Security is described as ensuring insurance is in place before residency permits are issued or renewed.

The basic policy has fixed features. The premium is Dh320 a year with no waiting period for pre-existing conditions, and the policy is valid for two years, with the second-year premium refundable if the visa is cancelled. Workers up to age 64 are eligible, and older workers must provide medical disclosures. Dependents can access the same benefits and pricing. Minimum benefits include inpatient care with a 20% co-payment capped at Dh500 per visit and an annual limit of Dh1,000, beyond which the insurer pays in full; outpatient care with a 25% co-payment capped at Dh100 per visit, and no co-payment for follow-up visits for the same condition within seven days; and medication with a 30% co-payment and an annual limit of Dh1,500. The network named in the article includes seven hospitals, 46 clinics and 45 pharmacies. Employers can buy through the DubaiCare Network or another accredited insurer. The article does not state penalties for non-compliance, and readers should check with the ministry.

These details are those reported at the launch and the plans and prices may have changed, so employers and workers should check current terms with the ministry or insurers. For employers, the practical steps are to confirm which of their workers are covered under existing policies, plan for renewals, and decide whether to offer better cover than the basic minimum. For residents, it is worth checking whether a basic policy gives enough protection and whether dependants are covered.

Taken together, the reports describe a market where mandatory cover is widening the base of insured people, while competition is lowering commercial prices and regulators are raising standards. The balance between affordable basic cover, adequate protection and financially strong insurers will shape the sector in the coming years.
image_alt: UAE Dubai health insurance and medical coverage market growth (illustrative)
key_points: Khaleej Times (February 17, 2026) projects UAE health and medical insurance at about $10.11 billion in 2026, growing at 8.26% a year to about $15.04 billion by 2031.

Marsh's index shows global commercial rates fell 4% in Q4 2025; in India, the Middle East and Africa rates fell 10%, Middle East property about 11%, UAE and Saudi D&O 15-20% and Middle East cyber 5-10%.
The IMF expects UAE growth of about 5% in 2026, and the Central Bank is implementing reforms under Federal Decree-Law No. 48 of 2023 covering solvency, governance and consumer protection.

Gulf News reports a nationwide employer-funded scheme began on January 1, 2025 for private-sector and domestic workers, extending mandatory cover to Sharjah, Ajman, Umm Al Quwain, Ras Al Khaimah and Fujairah; Abu Dhabi and Dubai already required it.

The basic policy costs Dh320 a year with no waiting period for pre-existing conditions, has co-payments of 20% inpatient, 25% outpatient and 30% on medication, and applies at permit renewal for workers with permits issued before 2025.
why_it_matters: Health insurance is mandatory for many UAE workers, so changes in cover rules and prices affect employers, residents and insurers alike. The market is growing, but commercial prices are falling, which makes the mix of regulation and competition important to watch.

title: Has Progressive Overtaken State Farm in Auto Insurance? What S&P's Estimate Shows and Why the Answer Depends on the Measure
summary: S&P Global estimates Progressive passed State Farm as the largest US private auto insurer in the 12 months to March 2026 by more than $1.57 billion, but AM Best's 2025 ranking of all property and casualty lines still has State Farm first at $113.8 billion.
description:
A headline that Progressive has overtaken State Farm as America's largest private passenger auto insurer has circulated since May. The claim is based on an estimate by S&P Global Market Intelligence, and it is correct on the measure S&P used, but it needs to be read alongside other rankings that use different measures and still put State Farm first. This article sets out what each source says. An earlier version of this article reported Progressive's first-quarter net income, revenue, underwriting margin, policy count and State Farm's policyholder dividend. The S&P page that was cited contains only a summary line, so those figures could not be confirmed from it and have been removed. The latest Progressive results are covered separately in our report on its third quarter.

What does S&P's analysis say? According to a summary of the analysis in the trade press, Progressive overtook State Farm as the largest US private auto insurer on a trailing 12-month basis ending March 31, 2026. It wrote more than $1.57 billion more in private direct premiums than State Farm over that period. The analysis used first-quarter 2026 statutory financial statements, the standard regulatory filings, together with what S&P describes as limited proprietary estimates. State Farm had held the top auto position since 1942, and Progressive has been second since 2022, ahead of GEICO, which had taken that place from Allstate in 2013. S&P's page for its separate first-quarter earnings recap, published on May 26, gives the sector context: a best first quarter in 25 years, with underwriting gains of $22.10 billion.

Now the other measure. AM Best's review of 2025 results ranks US property and casualty insurers by net premiums written across all their lines, not only auto. On that basis, State Farm leads with $113.79 billion, up 5.6% from 2024. Progressive is second with $83.15 billion, up 11.7%, and it passed Berkshire Hathaway Insurance, which includes GEICO and made $80.97 billion, up 0.8%. The rest of the top ten, as listed, are Allstate with about $56.7 billion, Travelers with $42.1 billion, USAA with $37.5 billion, Liberty Mutual with $37.2 billion, Chubb with $27.5 billion, Farmers with $21.5 billion and Hartford with $17.7 billion. AM Best's list mixes groups and companies without explaining the distinctions, and uses a different time period, a full year 2025 against S&P's twelve months to March 2026.

The two sets of figures are therefore not in conflict. State Farm remains larger in total, because it writes large amounts of homeowners and other insurance as well as auto. In private auto alone, S&P estimates Progressive has pulled ahead on a more recent twelve-month window, while State Farm's auto premiums have grown slowly. The difference between 'largest overall' and 'largest in auto' is the point: Progressive is a car insurer first, with fast growth, while State Farm is a diversified group.

Why did the lead change? The Coverager article, published on June 14, argues that State Farm lost momentum after years of underwriting problems and inadequate rates, and that the gap now reflects momentum more than size. That explanation is the author's characterisation and no source is cited for it. The facts the article does report are that State Farm's property and casualty underwriting result in the first quarter of 2026 moved to a $1.8 billion gain from a $5.1 billion loss a year earlier, and its auto result moved from a loss of $3.6 billion to a gain of $1.0 billion, with written premiums up 1.9% to $27.9 billion. For Progressive, the article reports a combined ratio of 90.2% and net income of $1.1 billion in April 2026, a record $1.5 billion of advertising in the first quarter, up 20%, and an expansion of its Snapshot telematics programme to 14 states. These figures cover different periods for the two companies, so they should not be compared directly.

Progressive's growth has continued. In the third quarter, which we report on elsewhere in this series, the company said it had 40.489 million policies in force at September 30, with direct auto up 8% and agency auto up 7% from a year earlier, and a combined ratio of 88.7. That is consistent with an insurer that continues to add customers faster than the market.

What does this mean for drivers? The size of an insurer does not tell you whether it offers the best price or service for your situation. Prices differ by state, driver profile and insurer. A more useful approach is to compare quotes from several companies, including regional carriers, review coverage and deductibles, and ask about discounts such as telematics programmes, which monitor driving habits in exchange for lower rates and may also affect renewals if the data show risky behaviour.

For the industry, the shift matters because auto insurance is a scale business: large insurers spend heavily on advertising, data and claims technology. If Progressive continues to grow faster than State Farm, it will gain even more data and spending power, while State Farm's recovery in underwriting results shows it still has capital and brand strength. Readers should treat any 'No. 1' claim as a snapshot that depends on the definition used.
source_name: Repairer Driven News (citing AM Best and S&P Global Market Intelligence) and Coverager
image_alt: US auto insurance market leadership Progressive versus State Farm (illustrative)
key_points: S&P Global Market Intelligence estimates Progressive overtook State Farm as the largest US private auto insurer on a trailing 12-month basis to March 31, 2026, writing more than $1.57 billion more in private direct premiums.
State Farm had held the top auto spot since 1942, according to S&P; Progressive has been No. 2 since 2022, ahead of GEICO.

AM Best's ranking by 2025 net premiums written across all property and casualty lines still has State Farm first at $113.79 billion (+5.6%), Progressive second at $83.15 billion (+11.7%) and Berkshire Hathaway Insurance, which includes GEICO, third at $80.97 billion.
S&P's analysis is an estimate based on Q1 2026 statutory statements and some proprietary estimates, not a reported result.
Coverager notes State Farm's Q1 2026 underwriting moved to a $1.8 billion gain from a $5.1 billion loss, with auto improving to +$1.0 billion from -$3.6 billion.
why_it_matters: Being the largest auto insurer affects pricing power, advertising spend and data scale. The story also shows why a headline such as 'No. 1' needs a measure and a period attached: premium type, time window and whether all lines are counted all change the answer.

title: Triple-I and Milliman: US Property and Casualty Underlying Growth Seen at -3.7% in 2026's First Half Despite the Best Underwriting Results in a Decade
summary: A Triple-I and Milliman briefing projects US property and casualty underlying growth of -3.7% in the first half of 2026, down from 1.6% in 2025, with recovery expected in 2027 and 2028 even as 2025 combined ratios were the lowest in over a decade.
description:
The US property and casualty insurance industry just had its most profitable underwriting year in more than a decade, but its growth is about to turn negative, according to the Insurance Information Institute (Triple-I) and the actuarial firm Milliman. Their briefing, titled "P&C Economics and Underwriting Projections: A Forward View," was reported by Reinsurance News on May 18, 2026. This article summarises the report as published. An earlier version of this article gave a net written premium growth figure of 3.6% for 2025 that does not appear in the report and has been removed. The only premium growth figure given in the source concerns personal auto, at 4.0%.

The headline number is underlying growth, which strips out the effect of price changes in a way that shows how much real business the industry is writing. The forecast is for underlying growth of negative 3.7% in the first half of 2026, down from 1.6% in 2025. The authors cite catastrophe exposure, inflationary pressures and rising claims costs as the drivers. They expect a recovery in 2027 and 2028, with continued pressure from economic uncertainty and elevated loss trends. The projection is a forecast and depends on assumptions about the economy and weather.

The profit side looks very different. The industry's net combined ratio, a measure that compares claims and expenses with premiums, was the lowest in more than a decade in 2025. Personal auto improved by 3.5 points from a year earlier to 91.8. Homeowners reached 88.1, the strongest underwriting result in more than ten years, despite catastrophe activity that included the Los Angeles wildfires. The report credits easing replacement-cost pressures and earlier pricing actions for the improvement. These figures are consistent with the S&P Global Market Intelligence analysis of the best first-quarter result in 25 years, which we have reported separately.

Premium growth in personal auto has slowed. Net written premium growth in personal auto was 4.0% in 2025, its lowest since 2021, and the briefing expects underwriting conditions to stay favourable into 2026. That fits with what insurers' own results show: Progressive's recent quarter, for example, showed policies growing faster than premiums, which usually means average prices are flat or falling.

Replacement costs are another focus. These are the costs of repairing or rebuilding insured property. The forecast is for replacement cost growth of 2.1% in the first half of 2026, unchanged from 2025. Patrick Schmid of Triple-I says that inflation in replacement costs has eased from its 2022 peak, but the forecasts show it re-accelerating through 2028 and eventually outpacing overall US inflation. For insurers, rising replacement costs mean higher claims in future even if current results look good, so profitable years can be followed by pressure.

Commercial lines show a split. General liability and commercial auto are expected to be the only major lines with a net combined ratio above 100 through 2026, meaning that they still lose money on underwriting, with gradual improvement in the years after. Jason Kurtz of Milliman says litigation pressures and claims severity trends continue to result in elevated loss costs. Workers' compensation is expected to be among the strongest performers from 2026 to 2028, with combined ratios in the low 90s. The National Council on Compensation Insurance, however, put the preliminary 2025 calendar-year workers' compensation combined ratio at 91, up about 5 points from the prior year, mainly because of higher loss and underwriting expense ratios. Donna Glenn of NCCI is quoted on that number.

The economy and employment provide context. The briefing says real GDP growth slowed to 2.0% in the first quarter of 2026 and consumer price inflation was 3.3% in March, above the Federal Reserve's long-term target. Insurance employment fell 1.8% year on year in March, underperforming the broader labour market. Michel Léonard of Triple-I said that insurers continue to operate in an environment marked by elevated catastrophe risk.

What should readers take from this? For consumers, strong industry profits do not guarantee lower premiums. Prices depend on expected future costs, and the report suggests costs will rise again as replacement costs accelerate. In auto and homeowners, there is room for competition, but liability costs are still high. For businesses buying commercial insurance, general liability and commercial auto are likely to stay under pressure, while workers' compensation looks more stable. For investors, the combination of record underwriting results and negative growth means earnings may be near a cyclical peak, although the report does not make that claim.

It is also worth noting what the report does not say. It does not give an industry-wide premium growth number, it does not forecast individual companies, and the first-half figure is a projection, not a result. Later data, including the third-quarter results of Travelers and Progressive covered in this series, show that margins remained strong through the autumn, so the forecast negative growth did not prevent profitable results. Readers who want the full forecast tables should consult the Triple-I and Milliman briefing itself.
image_alt: US insurance industry growth forecast and economic outlook 2026 (illustrative)
key_points: Triple-I and Milliman's briefing, reported on May 18, 2026, projects US P&C underlying growth of -3.7% in the first half of 2026, compared with 1.6% in 2025.
The 2025 net combined ratio was the lowest in more than a decade; personal auto improved 3.5 points to 91.8 and homeowners reached 88.1, the best in over ten years.
Auto net written premium growth slowed to 4.0%, its lowest since 2021, while replacement cost growth is forecast at 2.1% in the first half and is expected to re-accelerate through 2028.
General liability and commercial auto are expected to be the only major lines with a net combined ratio above 100 through 2026, while workers' compensation should stay in the low 90s.
NCCI put the preliminary 2025 workers' compensation combined ratio at 91, about 5 points higher than the year before; insurance employment fell 1.8% year on year in March.
why_it_matters: Strong underwriting profits do not mean strong growth. If underlying growth is negative, price increases are fading while costs keep rising, and the lines still losing money (liability and commercial auto) are the ones most likely to see firmer prices.
